title: Attacking the castled king

D0.outcome: Explains that a castled king's defence is its pawn cover and the pieces near it, and that an attack needs attackers to match the defenders.

D1.outcome: Counts the attackers who can reach and the defenders who can answer around a castled king, and names the weakened squares.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, chooses among bringing one more piece (opening a file), exchanging a defender, or not attacking, and recognises when the pawn cover has been loosened.

D3.outcome: Predicts how a defender's bishop or knight covering the holes refutes the attack, and checks the declined lines.

misconceptions: A sacrifice near the king always works.
Counting attackers is enough; the quality of the defenders does not matter.
conditions: In a king attack the number of attackers needed is compared with the defenders available; with exactly enough on both sides, moving any defender tips the balance.
The weak point is the pawn cover in front of the king, as after the king's knight pawn has advanced a square.
contrasts: The same pawn move, but a defender piece covers the key squares.
Counting defenders without checking which can really be removed.
A queenside pawn move that does not affect the king.

soft_prereq_notes.TAC.BACKRANK.D2: the back-rank weakness is the simplest castled-king attack
